issues.problem: L0 presents shared uses tied to natural expressions as Wittgenstein's settled argument. In the source it is "one possibility" (§244). The beetle point is conditional: it holds only if the word has a use at all.
issues.evidence: p. 95e: "Here is one possibility"; p. 106e: "what if these people's word 'beetle' had a use nonetheless? If so, it would not be as the name of a thing"

issues.problem: A rhetorical question with a hedge ("except perhaps as a joke") is turned into the plain assertion that "I know I'm in pain" says nothing more than that I am in pain. The bullet heading also calls the claim 'grammar, not a discovery' but cites only §246, which says "in one way false, in another nonsense"; the 'grammatical' wording is in §251.
The hedge "One would like to say" is dropped. The remark is presented as Wittgenstein's flat statement rather than as the temptation he then diagnoses.
issues.evidence: p. 99e: "One would like to say: whatever is going to seem correct to me is correct. And that only means that here we can't talk about 'correct'."

issues.problem: The condition "if the word has a use at all" is lost. The bullet says the thing is "not the name's object", but the source says that if the word has a use, it is not as the name of a thing.

The claim that "I am justified before myself" gives no real justification is not in the source. Wittgenstein asks what it means and says only that using a word without justification is not using it wrongfully.

"'Fiction' would be only a grammatical fiction" adds "only" and "would be". The remark answers an interlocutor's charge and says "If I speak of a fiction, then it is of a grammatical fiction". The phrase "the picture of it as the key to the word's use" is also not in the text.

Three intuition notes are stronger than the source. The check note has an "only if... could come out differently" condition not in the text. The doubt note has "only if... removed" where the source says "looks as if" and describes a temptation. The beetle note drops the "if the word has a use" condition and adds "meaning".
Wrong pages. §§265, 266 and 267 are all on p. 100e. The digest cites pp. 100e–101e for §265 and p. 101e for §§266–267. The same error is in the Canonical instances entry for imagined-timetable.

Wrong pages. §281 and the start of §282 are on p. 103e, and §282 ends on p. 104e. The digest cites p. 104e for §281 and 104e–105e for §282, with a confused note about page splitting. The Reading notes repeat the error.
§§296–298 are on p. 107e, not 108e. §303 is on p. 108e, not 109e. §304 runs from p. 108e to 109e. §280 is wholly on p. 103e. §288 is on p. 105e. §295 is on p. 107e. §274 has a typo "pp. 102e".

"That is not what I mean" and the following description are attributed to Wittgenstein. The text does not mark the speaker, and the sentence reads as the proposer of the private language. The voice is misattributed or at least unclear.
"The context of §244 suggests the implied answer is that I cannot" is the writer's own inference, not marked as such. The source gives no answer.
The source asks "Why can't a dog simulate pain? Is it too honest?" The digest turns this into the plain assertion "A dog cannot simulate pain".
"again and again" became "always". The hedge "perhaps" in §288 ("we would think, perhaps") was dropped.

"some of the directions" was shortened to "directions", which strengthens the claim.
The source hedge "seems" was dropped. The L2 bullet also states "is overstated" flatly.

"Share no common standard of comparison" is stronger than the source. The source says the paradigms can be compared well enough to be seen as rivals, and Kuhn accepts some shared criteria of theory choice (pp. 89–90, 91).
Several terms are undefined at first use: gestalt switch, crisis, candidate paradigm, invisible hand, punctuated equilibrium.

Several dropped hedges and conditions, and quotation marks put around author wording:
1. "capricious" and "leaps of faith" are not quoted in the source.
2. "some of the principles", "must often be traded off" and "could reliably" lost their qualifiers.
3. "seems to conflict" lost "seems".
4. "tend to bring" lost "tend to".
5. "no good theory of meaning exists" is stronger than "much success in developing a good theory".
6. The Smith/Kuhn critic is said to "excuse", but the source says "excuse and encourage".
7. "essential to science as we know it" is Godfrey-Smith's wording, not Kuhn's.
8. The "ideal paradigm" claim should be attributed to Kuhn.
9. "too tightly structured" is Godfrey-Smith's own view.
"Striking" is on p. 100, but the bullet cites p. 101.
Gould's "Eternal Metaphors in Paleontology" and the convergence remark (p. 101) are missing.
The digest says "opposite" effects. The source says only a "mismatch" between individual-level and whole-level characteristics, which is "apparent" and disappears.
"Page 116" and "(pdf 102–116 ...)" mix pdf and printed numbering, and the format checker flagged them. They should use printed numbers.

issues.problem: 'only if the system is stochastic' is stronger than the source. Ashby says only that a determinate system of finite size cannot have an infinitely long trajectory, so he moves to a more comprehensive non-determinate form. He also notes that 'stochastic' can include the determinate case, which makes 'only if' misleading.

'A coding always exists, as … examples show' turns the theorem's general claim into something two examples show. Ashby attributes the 'always exists' claim to Shannon's theorem. The a/d example illustrates no loss of information on merging, not the existence of a coding.
issues.evidence: p. 183 (theorem: a coding always exists); p. 184 (8-to-7 example); pp. 185–186 (a/d merge)

issues.problem: 'He suggests … probably a minor problem' adds a hedge ('probably') not in the source and drops the 'hardly arises' alternative. It also cites p. 177, which is about assumptions, for the error-free claim, and omits the stated reason (little restriction on channel capacity in the brain).
issues.evidence: p. 191: 'showing that the problem hardly arises, or that it is a minor, rather than a major, one'; p. 191 (little restriction in channel capacity)

issues.problem: 'exact arithmetic', 'fixed shares' and 'every insect' strengthen the source. The population is determinate only if large enough to be free from sampling irregularities, and in the example it tends to equilibrium; the source says 'the insects, which are moving incessantly'.
'Entropy is how many yes/no questions, on average, are needed to learn the next state' is not in the source, and it is not exactly true as stated.
issues.evidence: pp. 174–176 give the formula, the maximum log n and the weighted average, with no question-counting interpretation

issues.problem: 'entropy is the true "size" of a message source' and 'average length approaches the entropy' are slogans not in the source. The source only gives the coding and the 8-to-7 ratio.

The source says the assumptions are 'by no means so commonly fulfilled' in biology. The digest says 'by no means in biology', which strengthens the claim. The sentence also says 'the measure and theorems are … fulfilled', where the source speaks of their assumptions.
issues.evidence: p. 176: 'commonly fulfilled in telephone engineering but are by no means so commonly fulfilled in biological work'

issues.problem: The text 'from b, to b 0.6, to X 0.18...' is wrong. From b the probabilities are to X 0, to b 0.6, to c 0.4. The sentence also mixes row and column reading.

issues.evidence: p. 165: 'of the type we have considered throughout the book till now. The single-valued … transformation is thus simply a special, extreme, case of the stochastic'

issues.problem: The source says the probabilities depend 'in a constant way' on preceding states; the digest drops that condition.
issues.evidence: p. 171: 'transition probabilities depend in a constant way on what states preceded each operand'

issues.problem: 'A large population … settling to equilibrium' is stated generally. The source requires a population large enough to be free from sampling irregularities, and shows the settling for the insect example. 'Markov chain' also omits constancy.

'Redundancy exists when entropy is below its maximum' is stated generally. The source gives this only for a Markov chain; for sets of vectors it is the reducibility of components. 'Capacity is entropy per unit time' conflates the rate measure with the source entropy.
issues.evidence: p. 182 (Markov chain); p. 180 (capacity measured as a rate that depends on step speed and variety per step)

issues.problem: 'Capacity beyond the equivocation' is ambiguous. The theorem concerns an increase of capacity by an amount not less than E.
